I joined the Tsushima environmental volunteer workshop in the second semester of 2021.

We discussed environmental cleanup with students from Tsushima High School. Because it was during COVID, the event was online. First, we heard about marine waste in Tsushima. Then we split into groups of three high school students and four university students. We discussed ways to address the waste problem and whether we were interested in environmental issues.

I was surprised when we began the group discussion. Unlike me, who had joined mainly for exchange, the high school students were genuinely interested in the environment and had detailed knowledge. I had researched Tsushima's waste problem beforehand, but realized my preparation had been superficial. Their questions made me anxious, though I managed to respond reasonably and felt I had preserved some dignity as a university student.

As I had not previously paid much attention to environmental cleanup, I learned from the high school students and tried to remember their answers. One answer about marine waste still stands out: a kind of ocean rubbish bin was being developed as a new technology. It had never occurred to me, and I found it a strikingly simple but good solution.

That answer taught me that people with expertise can teach us regardless of age. Since then, I have worried less about age when getting to know people. I also struggled with difficult Japanese vocabulary and unfamiliar kanji, so I bought a JLPT N3 book and began studying kanji.
I became passive because I was very nervous at the exchange and disliked seeing myself that way. Wanting to change, I decided to join more exchange events. This workshop became the trigger.

I could only respond to the topic or the Japanese students' questions. The atmosphere did not improve, and all three group rounds went poorly.
I felt deeply frustrated by my lack of communication skills and became harder on myself. Already lacking confidence because of COVID and other circumstances, this made me feel even more discouraged.
I also felt my Japanese expression was limited, so I used the language exchange app HelloTalk to chat with many Japanese people and practice becoming familiar with expressions.
I joined an exchange with Kyushu Sangyo University on AI and language learning

After all the presentations, we went to a gathering and talked at three tables. I paid attention to atmosphere, initiative and how to ask questions. Although it felt awkward, I wanted to overcome shyness, so I tried to say something or ask a question. I thought about what questions would make others happy to keep talking. One-to-one conversation went well, but in larger groups I sometimes misspoke and briefly spoiled the atmosphere. I realized I needed to soften my forceful way of speaking.

Since then, I have gradually tried to find gentler alternatives before saying something too direct. I am more comfortable communicating in writing, so I practiced softer wording in chats. Now I also use AI repeatedly to practice speaking without letting emotion take over.
I wanted to make a better impression on people.

Students from Kyushu Sangyo University and Busan University of Foreign Studies presented. We were supposed to share a theme, but a misunderstanding resulted in different topics: free topics for Kyushu Sangyo and AI and language learning for Busan. Four teams from Kyushu Sangyo and three from Busan presented. I introduced how to learn Latin with ChatGPT.

I had three reasons to participate: to improve communication by joining more exchanges as I had decided in my second year, to build connections with Japanese people, and to use a valuable opportunity to improve spoken Japanese.

Choosing the topic was easy: I was studying Latin in class and already using ChatGPT to learn it. But that alone did not satisfy me. I had long struggled with presentations and admired speakers who could make listeners smile and stay engaged naturally. I thought about how to energize my presentation and built in a quiz with small prizes for correct answers.

Writing the quiz questions was not difficult, but I worried about presenting them naturally. I repeatedly pictured myself doing so and practiced speaking without a script. During the presentation I was nervous, yet delivered the quiz better than expected and everyone participated actively. However, the room soon became quiet again afterwards, so I began thinking about how to sustain the positive atmosphere in my next presentation.
